In most modern programming languages a variable is a named binding that refers to a value stored in memory. Scoping rules determine where in the source a variable is visible: block scope confines a binding to the nearest enclosing braces, while function scope makes it visible throughout the surrounding function. Lexical scoping resolves names based on the textual structure of the program, whereas dynamic scoping uses the call stack at runtime.

Type systems classify variables by the kind of values they may hold. A statically typed language like Rust or TypeScript checks types during compilation, catching many errors before the program runs. A dynamically typed language like Python defers those checks until runtime, trading some safety for flexibility. Strong typing prevents implicit conversion between unrelated types, while weak typing permits coercion. Together, scoping and typing form the backbone of how variables behave in practice.
